contentHtml:
What startup security in India actually requires

In short: A startup in India needs three things on a small budget: CERT-In's rules (report listed cyber incidents within 6 hours, keep logs for 180 days in India, sync clocks), the DPDP Rules' security safeguards that apply from May 2027, and a product built against the OWASP Top 10. CERT-In's free 15 controls for MSMEs turn that into a to-do list.

This guide was checked in November 2026, against CERT-In's directions and MSME controls, the DPDP Rules 2025 and the OWASP Top 10:2025. I am not a lawyer, and this is not legal advice. Where a rule has a date, I give it.

Security advice for startups usually swings between two bad extremes: "you are too small to be a target" and an expensive audit before the first customer. Neither fits. What fits is a short list of habits that cost mostly time, done in the right order, plus knowing what the law asks of you.

The four documents, side by side

Most of what a small Indian company must or should do comes from four documents. Here is what each one is and what it asks.

The four documents that shape startup security in India

DocumentIssued byBinding?What it asks of a startup
Cyber security directions under section 70B(6) of the IT Act, 28 April 2022CERT-InYes, for service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporate and government bodiesReport Annexure I incidents within 6 hours, keep ICT logs 180 days in India, sync clocks to NIC or NPL, name a point of contact
Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025MeitY, under the DPDP Act 2023Yes, with phased datesSecurity safeguards (Rule 6), breach notice to users and the Board, detailed Board report within 72 hours (Rule 7)
15 Elemental Cyber Defense Controls for MSMEs, version 1.0, 1 September 2025CERT-InGuidance15 controls with 45 baseline recommendations for self-assessment, and a baseline audit at least once a year
OWASP Top 10:2025OWASP FoundationNo, an awareness listThe ten most serious web application risks to design and test against

Source: CERT-In directions of 28 April 2022 and DPDP Rules 2025, Rule 1 and CERT-In MSME controls and OWASP Top 10:2025, read 16 November 2026.

Two of these are law and two are guidance. The guidance is where a small team gets the most for its time, because it tells you what to do on a Tuesday afternoon, not just what you will be fined for.

CERT-In: the rules you already have to follow

The CERT-In directions took effect in 2022 and have no startup exemption. They apply to "service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporate and Government organisations". In my reading, a private limited company running a website or app is a body corporate. The four duties that matter most:

  • 6-hour reporting. Report the incident types listed in Annexure I to CERT-In "within 6 hours of noticing such incidents or being brought to notice about such incidents", by email to incident@cert-in.org.in, phone (1800-11-4949) or fax.
  • 180 days of logs, in India. Enable logs of all ICT systems and keep them securely "for a rolling period of 180 days", maintained within Indian jurisdiction.
  • Clock sync. Connect systems to the NTP server of NIC or NPL, or servers traceable to them. Logs with wrong timestamps are hard to use in an investigation.
  • A point of contact. Designate a person to interface with CERT-In.

Annexure I has 20 incident types. The ones a typical startup can actually hit: unauthorised access of IT systems or data, website defacement, ransomware and other malicious code, phishing and identity theft, DDoS, attacks on e-commerce applications, data breach, data leak, attacks on digital payment systems, fake mobile apps, unauthorised access to social media accounts and attacks on cloud systems.

Two surprise founders. A data leak counts, not just a hack, so a public cloud bucket of customer invoices is reportable. And a hijacked company Instagram account is on the list too.

DPDP Rules: what changes in May 2027

The DPDP Rules were published on 14 November 2025. Rule 1 sets the dates: rules 1, 2 and 17 to 21 apply from publication, Rule 4 after one year, and rules 3, 5 to 16, 22 and 23 "eighteen months after the date of publication". That puts the security and breach rules in May 2027.

Rule 6 lists the minimum security safeguards. Read it as a checklist, because it is one:

  • Encryption, obfuscation, masking or virtual tokens for personal data.
  • Access control on the computer resources used by you or your data processor.
  • Logs, monitoring and review, so unauthorised access can be detected, investigated and fixed.
  • Measures to keep processing going if data is lost or compromised, "such as by way of data-backups".
  • Logs and personal data kept for one year, unless another law requires otherwise.
  • Security terms in your contracts with data processors. That includes your cloud host, your CRM and the agency that builds your app.
  • Technical and organisational measures to make sure all of this is actually observed.

Rule 7 covers breaches. You must tell each affected person "without delay", in plain language, what happened, what it means for them and what they can do. You must tell the Data Protection Board without delay, and send a detailed report "within seventy-two hours of becoming aware of the breach", unless the Board allows longer in writing.

The penalties are large. The Act's Schedule says failing to take reasonable security safeguards "may extend to two hundred and fifty crore rupees", and failing to notify the Board or affected people of a breach may extend to two hundred crore rupees. Those are ceilings, not fixed fines, but they explain why investors and enterprise customers now ask about this in due diligence.

CERT-In's 15 controls for MSMEs: the free to-do list

The most useful document for a small company is the one fewest founders have read. In September 2025 CERT-In published 15 Elemental Cyber Defense Controls for MSMEs. It applies to enterprises that meet the government's MSME classification, which covers most early-stage startups. It says MSMEs may use its 45 baseline recommendations for self-assessment, and may get a baseline audit from a CERT-In empanelled auditor at least once a year.

Here are the fifteen, with what I would do first for each on a small budget.

CERT-In's 15 elemental controls and a low-cost first step for each

ControlLow-cost first step
Effective asset managementOne sheet listing every laptop, phone, domain, cloud account, SaaS tool and who owns it
Network and email securitySPF, DKIM and DMARC on your domain; no shared mailbox passwords
Endpoint and mobile securityScreen lock, disk encryption and automatic updates on every work device
Secure configurationsNo default passwords; production database not open to the internet
Patch managementTurn on automatic updates; a monthly check of server and dependency updates
Incident managementA one-page plan: who decides, who reports to CERT-In in 6 hours
Logging and monitoringCloud and app logs switched on, kept 180 days, clocks synced
Awareness and trainingA 30-minute phishing and UPI fraud briefing for every new joiner
Third party risk managementA list of vendors who hold customer data, with security terms in contracts
Data protection, backup and recoveryAutomated backups stored separately, and one restore test a quarter
Governance and complianceOne named owner for security, reviewed at a monthly founders' meeting
Robust password policyA password manager for the team; no passwords in chat or spreadsheets
Access control and identity managementTwo-factor login on email, cloud, code and payments; remove leavers the same day
Physical securityLock screens and the server cupboard; no laptops left in the car
Vulnerability audits and assessmentsSelf-assess against the 45 recommendations; book an empanelled audit before a big launch

Source: CERT-In, 15 Elemental Cyber Defense Controls for MSMEs, version 1.0, read 16 November 2026.

The control names in the left column are CERT-In's. The first steps on the right are mine, chosen because they cost little beyond a few hours.

OWASP Top 10:2025: what to build against

CERT-In tells you how to run the company. The OWASP Top 10 tells your developers what to avoid in the product. The 2025 list is:

  • A01 Broken Access Control
  • A02 Security Misconfiguration
  • A03 Software Supply Chain Failures
  • A04 Cryptographic Failures
  • A05 Injection
  • A06 Insecure Design
  • A07 Authentication Failures
  • A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures
  • A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures
  • A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions

OWASP's introduction explains what changed. Broken access control stays at number one: on average 3.73% of applications tested had one or more of the 40 weaknesses in that category, and server-side request forgery is now rolled into it. Security misconfiguration moved up from fifth in 2021 to second. Software supply chain failures is an expansion of the old "vulnerable and outdated components", and OWASP says it has the fewest occurrences in the data but the highest average exploit and impact scores. Mishandling of exceptional conditions is new.

For a startup, the top three map neatly onto real mistakes I would look for first:

  • Access control: change the invoice or order ID in a URL or API call and see someone else's data. Every request has to check who is asking, on the server.
  • Misconfiguration: a staging server with real data, an admin panel at /admin with a default password, a storage bucket set to public.
  • Supply chain: a package nobody has updated in two years, or a new dependency added because a blog post said so. Know what you install.

Designing APIs so that the access check cannot be forgotten is cheaper than finding the bug later. We wrote about that in API design that ages well.

A budget security plan, step by step

Here is the order I would work through for a startup with a product live or about to launch. Most steps cost hours, not money.

Step 1. List what you have. Every device, domain, cloud account, code repository, payment account and SaaS tool, with an owner. You cannot protect what you have not written down, and this list is CERT-In's first control.

Step 2. Turn on two-factor login everywhere it matters. Email, cloud console, code hosting, domain registrar, payment gateway, social media. A hijacked social media account is a reportable incident; this is the cheapest way to avoid one.

Step 3. Give the team a password manager. Move shared logins out of WhatsApp groups and spreadsheets. Remove access for people who leave on their last day.

Step 4. Switch on logs and keep them 180 days. Cloud audit logs, server and application logs, admin panel logins. Check retention settings: many defaults are shorter. Sync server clocks to NIC or NPL NTP servers.

Step 5. Back up and test a restore. Automated database backups, stored away from the main account, and one real restore every quarter. A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a backup.

Step 6. Fix the OWASP top three in your product. Server-side access checks on every request, no default credentials or public buckets, and a dependency scan in your build.

Step 7. Write the one-page incident plan. Who decides something is an incident, who emails CERT-In within 6 hours, who tells customers, and, from May 2027, who reports to the Data Protection Board. Put the CERT-In email and phone number on it.

Step 8. Add security terms to vendor contracts. Rule 6 asks for them with data processors. Start with whoever hosts and builds your product.

Step 9. Self-assess, then audit when it is worth it. Go through CERT-In's 45 baseline recommendations yourself. Pay for an empanelled audit before an enterprise deal, a health or fintech launch, or a fundraise where it will be asked about.

Logging well is a topic of its own. If you are setting it up, observability before you need it covers what to capture.

Three worked examples

These are illustrative startups, made up to show how priorities shift by business type. They are not clients.

A B2B invoicing SaaS

Imagine a five-person Pune startup selling GST invoicing software to small traders. Each customer sees only their own invoices, so broken access control is the risk that ends the company: one trader reading another's sales. The first spend of time goes into server-side tenant checks on every API call and a test suite that tries to cross tenants.

Its customers are businesses, and enterprise buyers will send a security questionnaire. Having the CERT-In self-assessment done, logs kept for 180 days and a written incident plan answers half of it.

A clinic booking and records app

Imagine a Hyderabad health startup storing appointment history and lab reports for clinics. Health data raises the stakes of every DPDP safeguard. Encryption at rest, per-patient access checks, download links that expire and a log of who opened which report are the basics.

Here I would not wait for the self-assessment alone. An outside test before launch is worth it, and the vendor contracts with the clinics should say who does what when there is a breach.

A D2C brand on a hosted store

Imagine a Jaipur block-print brand on a hosted e-commerce platform, with payments through a gateway. The platform handles most product security. The risks left are the team's accounts: the store admin, the payment dashboard, the Instagram page and the email that resets all of them.

Two-factor login on all of those, a password manager, and removing an ex-employee's access on their last day cover most of the risk. The incident plan still matters: a hijacked Instagram account selling fake discounts in the brand's name is on CERT-In's list.

Five common mistakes

1. "We are too small to be a target." Most attacks are not aimed. Bots try default passwords and public buckets on everyone. CERT-In's directions also make no size exception for reporting.

2. Buying a tool before writing the list. A security product does not help if nobody knows which cloud accounts exist. Asset management is control number one for a reason.

3. Logs that are on but useless. Logs kept for 7 days, on servers with wrong clocks, in the same account an attacker would delete. CERT-In asks for 180 days and synced clocks; Rule 6 asks for a year for personal data access logs.

4. Treating the OWASP Top 10 as a certificate. It is an awareness list. Passing a scan for it does not mean the app is secure, and access control bugs often need a human to find them.

5. No one owns it. If security is everyone's job, the 6-hour report at 11 pm on a Saturday is nobody's. Name the person.

A monthly 30-minute security check

  • Review who has access to email, cloud, code and payments. Remove anyone who has left or changed role.
  • Check that automatic updates ran on laptops, phones and servers. Update outdated dependencies.
  • Confirm logs are still flowing and retained for 180 days.
  • Confirm the last backup ran. Once a quarter, restore one.
  • Check no storage bucket, database or admin panel has become public.
  • Re-read the incident plan. Is the CERT-In contact person still at the company?
  • Note one item from CERT-In's 45 recommendations to fix before next month.

For staff devices, CERT-In also runs the Cyber Swachhta Kendra, its botnet cleaning and malware analysis centre, which links to free bot removal tools from antivirus companies. It is worth a bookmark for the team.

Where outside help fits

Most of this list is habit, and a founder can run it. Where outside help earns its fee is the product itself: access control, secure configuration and a test before launch. If you are building a product and want security scoped in from the start, our ₹3,500 requirement analysis is a call with the people who will build it, the requirements worked through, and a written fixed quotation and timeline before any build starts (see how it works). Code, cloud and credentials stay in your company's name, which matters for Step 1. For protecting the business more broadly, see our business protection services.
